  • Imaging Science Foundation (ISF)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Fills the entire screen (or, in a multi-column/row layout, every cell) with a single flat color. It is the simplest possible pattern, and precisely because of that, one of the most diagnostic: with no gradient, no lines and no geometry to distract the eye, any deviation from a perfectly flat, uniform field stands out immediately.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description Color The flat color to display. Available presets: black, white, red, green, blue, magenta, yellow, cyan.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A display should reproduce a flat color field as, well, flat — the same luminance and chromaticity across the entire panel. In practice, backlight design (edge-lit vs. full-array), panel manufacturing tolerances, and video processing can all introduce visible non-uniformity that a full-color image would normally mask.

  • Black is the most sensitive test for backlight bleed and IPS glow, since even small amounts of stray light are highly visible against a true black field.
  • White reveals uneven backlight brightness (clouding) and color-uniformity issues (a tint shifting from one edge to another).
  • Red / Green / Blue in isolation reveal single-channel uniformity problems and are also the standard way to check for stuck or dead sub-pixels, which are invisible in a busy image but obvious as a single wrong-colored dot on a flat field.
  • Cyan / Magenta / Yellow (secondary colors) can reveal channel-mixing or convergence issues that a primary color alone would not show.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Set the pattern to Single Color from the Pattern menu.
  2. Pick a color (start with black and white, then check the primaries individually if you suspect a sub-pixel or uniformity issue).
  3. Show it fullscreen (View → Show Pattern).
  4. Sit at a normal viewing distance and scan the whole screen, corner to corner — dead/stuck pixels and backlight bleed are both easiest to spot at the edges and corners.
  5. For backlight bleed specifically, dim the room lights: bleed is far more visible in a dark environment than under normal office lighting.

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: A perfectly uniform field, same brightness and color from edge to edge, with no visible dots, patches, or gradient across the panel.

docs.title: Dead or stuck pixels
docs.text: A single pixel (or sub-pixel) that stays black (dead) or shows a fixed color regardless of the field being displayed (stuck). Most visible against a contrasting flat field — check each primary color in turn.

docs.title: Backlight bleed / clouding
docs.text: Patches of lighter gray or visible light leakage, usually along the edges or corners, most visible on a black field in a dark room. Common on LCD panels, especially edge-lit ones.

docs.title: Color non-uniformity
docs.text: A visible tint shift across the panel on a white field (e.g. slightly warmer on one side, cooler on the other) — a sign of backlight or panel color-uniformity variance.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Let the display warm up for a few minutes before judging uniformity — brightness and color can drift noticeably during the first minutes after power-on, especially on LED-backlit panels. For a more rigorous uniformity check across a grid of screen zones rather than a single full-screen field, see Uniformity, Black Uniformity and White Uniformity in the reference library.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The sRGB pattern verifies the monitor's ability to reproduce the Standard RGB color space.

sRGB is the default color space used by:

  • Windows
  • Internet
  • Office applications
  • Most consumer software

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Web graphics
  • General photography
  • Office applications
  • Consumer displays

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Verify:

  • primary colors
  • neutral gray
  • saturation
  • color transitions

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The display should accurately reproduce the entire sRGB gamut without clipping.

docs.title: Oversaturation
docs.text: Colors appear excessively vivid.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Uniformity patterns reveal brightness and color variations across the display surface.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Panel inspection
  • Manufacturing QA
  • Display aging analysis

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect:

  • center
  • edges
  • corners

The display should appear visually uniform.

docs.title: Clouding
docs.text: Localized brighter areas.

docs.title: Backlight Bleeding
docs.text: Light leakage near the panel edges.

docs.title: Dirty Screen Effect
docs.text: Uneven luminance causing visible patches.

docs.title: Tinting
docs.text: Color shifts across different panel regions.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Uniformity evaluation should be performed in a dark room.

Allow the monitor to warm up before testing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Viewing Angle patterns evaluate image stability when the observer changes position.

This test is particularly important for LCD technologies.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Panel comparison
  • Display quality evaluation
  • Installation verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe the display from:

  • front
  • left
  • right
  • above
  • below

Evaluate:

  • brightness
  • contrast
  • color shift

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The White Level pattern verifies that the display reproduces highlight information without clipping.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Contrast adjustment
  • HDR evaluation
  • Video calibration

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The brightest white should remain distinguishable from the adjacent lighter gray levels.

No highlight detail should disappear.

docs.title: White Clipping
docs.text: Several bright levels merge into pure white.

docs.title: Blooming
docs.text: Bright areas illuminate surrounding pixels.

docs.title: Tone Compression
docs.text: Highlights lose detail.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: White Level should always be adjusted after Black Level.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• VESA DisplayHDR
  • ITU-R BT.709

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: White Uniformity evaluates the consistency of brightness and color across a white screen.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Professional monitor evaluation
  • Print proofing
  • Photography
  • Color grading

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Display a full white image.

Inspect:

  • brightness
  • tint
  • luminance distribution

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The display should appear:

  • evenly illuminated
  • neutral
  • free of visible patches

docs.title: Corner Darkening
docs.text: Corners appear darker than the center.

docs.title: Color Tint
docs.text:
Some regions become:

  • warmer
  • cooler
  • green
  • magenta

docs.title: Bright Spots
docs.text: Localized brighter areas become visible.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Professional graphics monitors usually specify uniformity compensation.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text: • ISO 12646

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ISO
  • EIZO Technical Library

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Zone Plate pattern evaluates frequency response, scaling algorithms and aliasing.

It contains concentric sinusoidal structures with continuously increasing spatial frequency.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Image processing evaluation
  • Scaling verification
  • Camera testing
  • Video processor validation

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A correct system should display:

  • smooth concentric rings
  • stable image
  • no false structures

docs.title: Aliasing
docs.text: False patterns appear at high spatial frequencies.

docs.title: Ringing
docs.text: Artificial oscillations appear around transitions.

docs.title: Moiré
docs.text: Interference patterns become visible.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Zone Plate patterns are extremely sensitive to resampling algorithms.

They are commonly used to evaluate image processing pipelines.

docs.title: First Start
docs.text: When PatternTester starts, the Main Window appears — a compact control panel with a menu bar at the top and, below it, a panel showing the parameters for whichever pattern is currently selected.

docs.title: Selecting a Monitor
docs.text: If more than one display is connected, choose the target monitor from Display → Monitor before showing a pattern fullscreen. Not sure which physical screen is which? Use View → Identify Monitors — see Identifying Monitors in the User Guide.

docs.title: Choosing and Configuring a Pattern
docs.text:
1. Pick a test from the Pattern menu.
  2. The configuration panel below the menu bar updates automatically to show that pattern's parameters (for example, gamma value and grid size for Gamma; direction for a gradient).
  3. Adjust the parameters as needed — changes apply live once the pattern is shown.

docs.title: Showing and Leaving Fullscreen
docs.text:
• View → Show Pattern displays the pattern fullscreen, above every other window, on the monitor selected in step 1.
  • To go back to the controls, right-click anywhere on the fullscreen pattern, or untick View → Show Pattern again from the main window.

docs.title: Before You Start Evaluating
docs.text:
For more consistent results:

  • Let the monitor warm up for a few minutes.
  • Disable dynamic contrast and automatic/adaptive brightness where possible.
  • Reset any picture "enhancement" modes (sharpening, motion smoothing) to neutral.
  • Use the monitor's native resolution.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: The full User Guide covers every menu in detail, including Settings (theme, startup behavior, save mode) and the Info Monitor / Identify Monitors panels.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Download PatternTester-Setup-<version>.exe from the latest GitHub release.
  2. Run it and follow the setup wizard — choose your language, accept the GPL-3.0 license, and install.
  3. The installer is self-contained: the .NET runtime is bundled with the application, so nothing else needs to be installed separately.
  4. At the end of setup you can optionally view the changelog and known-issues notes, and launch PatternTester immediately.

After installation, PatternTester is available from the Start Menu and (if selected during setup) a Desktop shortcut.

docs.title: Building the installer yourself
docs.text: See the Developer Guide if you'd rather build the installer from source instead of downloading a release.

docs.title: Linux (Debian / LMDE)
docs.text:
A prebuilt .deb package is produced from the same source using the standard Debian packaging tools. To install one:

sudo apt install ./PatternTester-<version>-amd64.deb

To build the package yourself from source (for example on LMDE 7), see README_DEBIAN.md in the repository — it covers installing the .NET 10 SDK, the required packaging tools (dpkg-dev, fakeroot), and the full dotnet publish + dpkg-deb --build sequence used to produce the .deb.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
• Windows: run a newer PatternTester-Setup-<version>.exe; it installs over the existing version.
  • Linux: install a newer .deb the same way as above; apt handles the upgrade.

Your configuration (last-used pattern/monitor, theme, saved defaults) is stored separately from the application files and is preserved across updates — see Settings in the User Guide for the exact file location.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Windows: Settings → Apps → PatternTester → Uninstall (or use the shortcut created in the Start Menu group).

Linux: 

sudo apt remove patterntester

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
PatternTester is a monitor test pattern generator for display evaluation, calibration checks and quality control. It can be used with LCD, OLED, MiniLED and CRT monitors, TVs, projectors, video processors and capture devices — anything that accepts a standard video signal from a Windows or Linux PC.

The application generates fullscreen test patterns to help evaluate geometry, gamma, color reproduction and general display behavior.

docs.title: Main Features
docs.text:
• Fullscreen pattern generator, one monitor at a time or across several simultaneously
  • Multi-monitor support, including mixed display-scaling setups on Windows
  • Native resolution output on the target monitor
  • 11 built-in test patterns (see the Pattern Reference)
  • Light and dark application theme
  • Italian and English interface, with additional languages addable via a simple JSON file (see External Languages)

docs.title: Intended Audience
docs.text:
• Home users and enthusiasts
  • Photographers and video editors
  • Display reviewers
  • Service technicians and AV integrators
  • Quality assurance / quality control workflows

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 10/11 or a Linux distribution with a graphical desktop (X11-based; see Linux notes)
  • A GPU/driver capable of the monitor's native resolution
  • No internet connection required — PatternTester runs entirely offline
